result.summary: Jupiter tells the gods how he travelled through Arcadia and was tested by King Lycaon, who served him human flesh. Jupiter destroyed the house, and Lycaon fled and turned into a wolf. Jupiter then says the whole world is wicked and he means to punish all men.

scenes.title: Argument of the Fable
scenes.summary: A heading states that Lycaon tests Jupiter with a murdered hostage and is turned into a wolf.

scenes.title: Lycaon's Test and Jupiter's Fire
scenes.summary: Jupiter arrives in Arcadia and is worshipped by the people, but Lycaon mocks them. He plots to kill the god in his sleep and serves a murdered hostage. Jupiter burns the house down.
scenes.stakes: Jupiter risks death in his sleep; Lycaon risks divine punishment for his impiety and murder.

scenes.title: Lycaon Becomes a Wolf
scenes.summary: Lycaon flees to the countryside, howls, cannot speak, and turns into a wolf that keeps his old fierceness.
scenes.stakes: Lycaon loses his human form and speech.

scenes.title: Jupiter Condemns Mankind
scenes.summary: Jupiter says one house fell, but all the earth is full of wickedness, and he resolves to punish all men.

characters.name: Erinnys
characters.description: Fury of vengeance, here a figure for savage wickedness reigning on earth

alias_notes.explanation: Jupiter refers to himself as a god in the narration and heading.

notable_quotes.reason: Jupiter declares his resolve to punish all humankind, setting up the Flood.

analysis.text: Lycaon's impiety and cannibal feast show human moral decay and justify the coming Flood. His wolf shape mirrors his savage nature.
The tale draws on Arcadian cult legends about Lycaon and werewolf-like transformation, linked to Mount Lycaeus.

legacy.text: The Lycaon story is a source of the word lycanthropy, meaning transformation of a man into a wolf, and fed later werewolf lore.

fun_facts.text: The Greek word for wolf is lykos, which links to the name Lycaon and Mount Lycaeus.

language_notes.text: Mænalus, Lycæus and Cyllene are mountains of Arcadia in southern Greece, associated with wild country and with the gods Pan and Mercury.
Tyrant here simply means a king or absolute ruler, not necessarily a cruel one, though Lycaon proves cruel.
The Molossians were a people of Epirus in northwest Greece; the hostage was sent as a pledge of peace.
Household Gods (Lares and Penates) were the spirits guarding a Roman home; their ruin shows the whole house was defiled.
Erinnys is a Fury, a goddess of vengeance and crime; here she stands for wickedness spread through the world.

context_notes.text: This heading is the translator's summary. Jupiter tells the story to the gods in council, which is why the narration is in the first person.
Gods often travelled disguised among mortals, and hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty. Lycaon's behaviour violates it.
Serving human flesh to a guest is a shocking crime in Greek myth, as in the stories of Tantalus and Thyestes.

literary_notes.text: Lycaon's test of divinity is itself the proof of his impiety; the god he doubts is the guest he plans to kill.
Overthrowing a house with avenging flames is a grand image of divine wrath, and calling the household gods 'worthy of their master' adds bitter irony.
The change is told in quick, plain clauses, with the man's body turning into the wolf's, which makes the transformation seem natural and inevitable.
'The same' recurs, stressing that the outward change leaves Lycaon's cruel nature unchanged: his form now fits his character.
